label: Symplectic Forms
notes: Welcome to Lecture One, covering printed pages one through six. The whole lecture grows from one linear-algebra fact: a skew pairing with no kernel forces an even dimension and a standard model. We promote that fact to manifolds and meet our first three examples before the hour is out.

label: Skew-Symmetric Bilinear Forms
notes: Start purely algebraically. A bilinear map on a vector space is skew when swapping arguments flips the sign, so every vector pairs to zero with itself. Emphasize that skewness already feels like oriented area, which is exactly the geometric reading we will lean on for the rest of the course.

label: The Standard Normal Form
notes: This is the structural theorem of the day. By a Gram-Schmidt style induction every skew form splits into a kernel block plus area pairs. Stress that the kernel dimension and the number of pairs are basis-independent invariants, and that the paired part always has even rank no matter how the form looked initially.

label: Symplectic Vector Spaces
notes: Nondegeneracy is the no-kernel condition: the only vector orthogonal to everything is zero. Equivalently the induced map to the dual space is an isomorphism. Point out that nondegeneracy plus the normal form immediately forces even dimension and hands us a symplectic basis identifying the space with the standard model.

label: The Standard Form on R^{2n}
notes: Here is the prototype every later example imitates. Pair the coordinates into conjugate planes and let omega-zero be the sum of the elementary area forms. Walk through the matrix: identity and minus-identity blocks. This is the concrete object the abstract symplectic basis was secretly describing all along.

label: Conjugate Planes and Oriented Area
notes: Spend time on the picture. The form reads off signed area in each conjugate plane and ignores cross terms between different planes. Have students compute omega-zero on two sample vectors so the determinant-as-area interpretation lands. This visual is the intuition they should carry into every nondegeneracy check.

label: Subspaces and the Symplectic Orthogonal
notes: Introduce the orthogonal of a subspace under the form and the dimension count that always holds. The four names follow from comparing a subspace to its orthogonal. Lagrangian, the half-dimensional self-orthogonal case, is the one that dominates the subject, so flag it as the case to remember.

label: Symplectic Manifolds
notes: Now go smooth. A symplectic manifold carries a two-form that is closed and nondegenerate at every point. Explain why both conditions matter: nondegeneracy is the pointwise linear-algebra input, closedness is the differential condition that later yields Darboux's theorem and the whole rigidity of the theory.

label: First Examples
notes: Give the three founding examples. Euclidean space with the standard form, any oriented surface with an area form, and the two-sphere whose form pairs tangent vectors by the triple product with the outward normal. The sphere is the first genuinely curved example, so let students dwell on it.

label: Volume and Symplectomorphisms
notes: Two payoffs of nondegeneracy. The top power of omega divided by n factorial is a nowhere-vanishing volume form, so symplectic manifolds are orientable. A symplectomorphism is a diffeomorphism pulling one form back to the other, and its linearization must preserve the pairing, which the matrix residual checks.

label: Recap and Look Ahead
notes: Close by tracing the arc: skew forms, normal form, nondegeneracy, the standard model, then manifolds and maps. Preview that Darboux's theorem will say dimension is the only local invariant, so all the local complexity lived in the linear algebra we did today. Send them to the exploration prompt.
